title: Who&When Pro: Can LLMs Really Attribute Failures in AI Agents?
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: A benchmark spans many source datasets, modalities and agent topologies, with concrete examples of where agents fail.
layout: Central two-ring wheel with four corner example panels; radial reading
description: A circular dual-ring chart sits at the center, with the title 'Who & When Pro' in the middle. The inner ring splits 26 source benchmarks into 9 task categories (Video QA, Embodied, STEM, Data Science, Deep Search, Coding, Image QA, MM-DeepSearch, GUI). The outer ring lists the benchmark names, such as LV-Bench, GPQA, MATH, HumanEval and GAIA. Colors mark the modality: red/pink for video, blue for text, orange/yellow for image and GUI. Four rounded corner panels show annotated agent traces. Video QA: a planner and reasoner misidentify a frame. Coding: Architect, Engineer and Reviewer agents with a planning error. Image QA: a chart misread. Web: goal drift while comparing watches. Each panel has robot icons, speech boxes, pink or blue arrows and a red-highlighted decisive error step. An orange warning box labels the error agent and type. The eye goes first to the colorful wheel.
caption: \textbf{Overview of \ours{}. } The inner ring groups 26 source benchmarks into 9 task categories. The outer ring maps each benchmark to its modality (\textbf{text, image, video}). Four corner panels illustrate failure attribution examples across modalities and agent topologies. (Top left) a \textbf{video} agent misidentifies a frame. (Top right) a multi-agent \textbf{coding} pipeline adopts a suboptimal architecture. (Bottom left) an \textbf{image} QA agent misreads a chart trend. (Bottom right) a \textbf{web} agent drifts from the user task. The decisive failure step are highlighted in each panel. Trace contents are summarized for illustration purposes and do not reflect the full agent outputs.
abstract: Automated failure attribution uses LLMs to identify where and why agentic systems fail. As agents become more capable, their failures become subtler, making automated attribution increasingly important. We introduce Who&When Pro, a large-scale benchmark for automated failure attribution in agentic systems. Using a strictly controlled pipeline that injects a failure only after exactly replaying a successful prefix, we construct 12,326 failed trajectories with golden labels across 3 modalities and 26 benchmarks covering various scenarios. Beyond benchmarking, we conduct extensive experiments and analyses, revealing systematic patterns in how models attribute failures across modalities, protocols, and model families, and providing empirical guidance for future automated failure attribution systems.
